meta.about: Every registered prompt, reviewed and given a verdict. Reference excerpts are verbatim quotes from the leaked system prompts of two frontier coding agents (the newest two available), machine-verified against those files — they are prior art to synthesise from, not text to copy. Every claim carries the code reference it came from so it can be re-checked.

verdicts.core: Load-bearing. Keep it. Any action here is a refinement, not a question about whether it should exist.
verdicts.optional: Works, costs little, and nothing breaks without it. Cut it if you want a leaner prompt; keep it if the feature it serves is live.
verdicts.delete: Should not exist. It duplicates something else, or serves a feature you have parked. Empty it here, or remove its call site for every machine.
verdicts.merge: The right content in the wrong place. Fold it into the named prompt, then empty this one.

meta.addressed: A note turns green once the prompt no longer matches reviewedHash — the snapshot it was written against. Disabling also counts as addressed.
meta.quoteAudit: All reference excerpts were checked verbatim against the two source files on 2026-07-29: 12 chunks, 0 mismatches. Quotes that turned out to come from older revisions or from a bundled skill were removed rather than re-attributed.
meta.principle:
Two rules govern every action in this review.

1. ADD A LINE, NEVER A ROUND. If a rule is worth having, it belongs inside a prompt that is already being sent — a bullet in an existing section, a clause in a tool description. A new reminder or a new pre-layer buys the same words at the price of a full model call, every time it fires. Prompt text is nearly free; round trips are not.

2. WE ARE NOT COPYING. The reference is prior art for wording and placement, not a target to converge on. Several things this engine does have no counterpart there and are better — they are marked OURS below and must survive any edit. Where a reference line and one of ours say the same thing, ours stays.
meta.audit: Checked on 2026-07-29 whether each reference rule was genuinely absent here. Six of nine were already present, several stated more strongly — those recommendations were withdrawn. Only three real gaps remain: scope fidelity, anti-rumination, and the task-continuation rule.
meta.purpose: Prompt Lab is where this agent gets designed, not where it gets compared. Every prompt the engine sends is listed here with what it is for, where it fires, and what it costs — so the whole behaviour of the product can be reasoned about in one place and changed in one place. The reference excerpts are research: evidence about what a mature harness found worth saying, and where it chose to say it. They are not a specification to converge on. Several things this engine does are already better, and those are marked OURS.

reference.text:
## Corrections
Avoid unnecessary or excessive self-correction. Only correct an earlier statement in your user-facing text when the error would change the user's code, conclusions, or decisions. State corrections plainly and concisely, and continue the task; combine multiple corrections rather than enumerating them all. For slips that change nothing for the user, simply make the correction and move on - no need to note it explicitly. Don't add apologies or preambles, don't be overly self-critical, and don't ruminate or give a detailed account of the mistake or tally past errors. Sometimes, other agents will report incorrect or misleading results - don't always take them at face value immediately. If other agents correct your statements and they are right, then simply update your approach without narrating too much about the correction to the user. This instruction does not apply to thinking blocks.

A follow-up question about your earlier work is not, by itself, a signal that you got something wrong — answer what was asked. A statement that was accurate needs no correction: don't re-audit how you phrased it, how you verified it, or limits you already stated. When the user does point to a real error, correct it plainly as above.

system.communication.ours: The markdown table contract, with a worked example. The reference has nothing like it, and a malformed table is a visible defect in your workbench.

Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target — if what you find contradicts how it was described, or you didn't create it, surface that instead of proceeding. reference.label: Reference harness
reference.text:
## Delivering work
Do ordinary work as asked, acting on the actual request rather than on speculation about what lies behind it. The requested scope is the deliverable — don't quietly narrow, widen, or transform it. Interpret ambiguity the way a careful colleague would: make routine judgment calls yourself, and check in only when different readings would lead to materially different work. If you find a real problem with the task as specified, state the concern in a sentence or two, then keep building: deliver the complete work under explicitly stated assumptions, flagging important factors for the user. Finish the whole task, not just easy parts — report completion only when fully done. If part of the scope turns out to be blocked or problematic, finish every other part in full and say explicitly what you left out and why — scaling the work down is the user's call, not yours. Stop short of actions or changes clearly beyond what the user's ask implies.

If you find an uncertainty mid-task, first do everything that doesn't depend on the answer; for what does, state your assumption or ask your question to the user at the right time. Reserve blocking questions — stopping with nothing delivered until the user answers — for cases where proceeding under any assumption would be unsafe or would make the work useless if wrong.

system.autonomy.ours: 'When you have what you need to act, act' plus the thinking-aloud exception — deliver an assessment and stop rather than fixing uninvited. The reference has the first; the exception is yours and it prevents a whole class of unwanted edits.

finishing.runtime-evidence.problem:
654 tokens. Three problems.

1. Step 4 says 'You have no eyes here'. That is false: `read.ts:84` returns PNG as an image block and `ToolResultPart` carries `type: "image"`. A vision model can be shown a screenshot today. The agent reads this as 'visual verification is impossible', stops looking, falls back to type-checking, and reports success on UI work it never saw.

2. The escape clause names 'a console, a display, a device' as a legitimate stopping point. In a desktop UI app that fires on nearly every frontend task.

3. Step 1 tells the agent to run the build, then says the build is not evidence. It costs a command and settles nothing.
finishing.runtime-evidence.action:
Change step 4 to 'Never claim an observation you did not make.' — a rule about honesty, not about capability. Narrow the escape clause to credentials and external services; drop 'a display'. Cut step 1. Merge the two closing paragraphs. Target ~450 tokens.

Longer term, follow the reference's placement: move visual verification into an on-demand skill so it costs nothing until a UI task needs it.

workOrder.about: Ordered so that nothing is emptied before its replacement exists. Every merge edits the RECEIVING prompt first, then clears the source — do it the other way round and the rule is gone from the prompt set for as long as the gap lasts. A step turns green only when its own test passes — the specific edit landed, or the source prompt is empty — not merely because the prompt was touched at some point. A step whose test can never pass, because you decided against the edit or withdrew the step, can be marked done by hand: it then counts as done but stays amber, never green, so the board still shows which steps were proven and which were asserted.
